newsitem.title: GERMANY: German court jails guerrilla for life.
newsitem.headline: German court jails guerrilla for life.

text.p: A German court on Tuesday sentenced an urban guerrilla charged with killing two U.S. soldiers and attempting to murder Hans Tietmeyer, president of Germany's central bank, to life imprisonment.

Birgit Hogefeld, a member of the left-wing RAF group which waged a sporadic war of killing and kidnapping against the establishment in the 1970s and 1980s, received the sentence after last-minute appeals to hear more witnesses were rejected by the five-judge court.
Hogefeld said in court on October 29 she believed the court had made up its mind before her trial, which lasted for more than 100 court sessions, began in November 1994.
Her lawyers on Tuesday sought to delay the verdict after another Red Army Faction (RAF) suspect, Christoph Seidler, said in a weekend magazine interview he was ready to surrender.
Seidler is wanted for the 1989 assassination of then Deutsche Bank chief executive Alfred Herrhausen, considered one of Germany's most spectacular political killings of recent times.
Lawyers said Seidler, who spent the years between 1987 and 1992 in Lebanon, might have information to clear Hogefeld.

Hogefeld, 40, was convicted of involvement in the 1985 bombing of a United States air base in Frankfurt in which a soldier and a civilian were killed. Another soldier was killed before the bombing so that his identity card could be used.
She was also convicted for taking part in a 1988 attempt to kill Tietmeyer, who was then a finance ministry state secretary and is now president of the Bundesbank.

The court did not issue a judgment on a charge of murder linked to her arrest in June 1993 when police ambushed her and companion Wolfgang Grams at a railway station in the north German town of Bad Kleinen.

Grams shot policeman Michael Newrzella and then himself in a chaotic shootout after Hogefeld had already been seized. Activists claimed police shot Grams in cold blood but independent inquiries found that he shot himself in the head.
Prosecutors had charged Hogefeld with Newrzella's murder, arguing that she was jointly responsible because she and Grams both carried guns and had agreed to use them to resist arrest.
She had told the court in a final statement that the RAF now belonged to a "bygone era" and should dissolve itself and that the armed struggle had been in error.
